title: Frumentius in Ethiopia
hookLine: a boy spared when his ship is attacked helps raise a prince, and comes back a bishop

lines: A SHIP PUTS IN AT A HARBOR.
cards: Two boys are sitting under a tree with their books, studying, while the grown-ups go ashore for water. Remember that tree. After days in the cold north, the map swings far to the south.

A teacher from the city of Tyre is sailing home with two young relatives, Frumentius and his brother Aedesius. The ship puts in at a harbor. And the people there, the old account says, are at odds with the Romans.
They attack, and everyone on the ship is killed, except two boys found under a tree, reading.

teach.h: THE BOYS GO TO THE KING.
teach.b: The story is told by Rufinus, a church historian who says he heard it from Aedesius himself, years later. The boys are taken to the king, and the king likes them. Aedesius becomes his cupbearer.
Frumentius, the sharper of the two, is put in charge of the royal records and accounts. Then the king dies. He leaves a young son, and before he dies he sets the two foreigners free.
But the queen asks them to stay and help run the kingdom until the prince is grown, and they do. Frumentius uses his position quietly.

He looks for Christian merchants passing through from the Roman world, and helps them set up places to meet and pray. When the prince comes of age, the brothers hand everything back and leave. Aedesius goes home to Tyre.
Frumentius goes to Alexandria, to the bishop there, Athanasius, and says: there are Christians in that land, and they need a bishop.
Athanasius answers, in effect: who could we find better than you? He makes Frumentius a bishop and sends him straight back. The old writers call the place India, a word they used loosely.
Historians connect it with the kingdom of Aksum, in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea.
Ethiopian Christians remember Frumentius as their own, and call him Abba Salama, father of peace.
In the Ethiopian Orthodox church, the altar holds a tabot, a tablet that stands for the tablets of the covenant kept in the ark. Ethiopian tradition says the ark itself rests in Ethiopia.
A church of the ark, begun with two boys under a tree.

how: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Christians honor Frumentius as Abba Salama, and their churches keep a tabot, a consecrated tablet, on the altar; at the feast of Timkat, the tabots are carried in procession.

o: the king of Aksum who freed two foreign boys
a captive boy who came back to Aksum as a bishop
a merchant who carried the ark into Ethiopia

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.

s: the boys were found under a tree, reading
everyone else on the ship was killed. the boys were found studying and taken to the king.
Frumentius went home to Tyre once he was free
the brothers stayed to help the queen. later Aedesius went home, and Frumentius went to Alexandria.
Frumentius asked Athanasius to make him a bishop
he asked Athanasius to send a bishop. Athanasius chose Frumentius.

games.q: you're Frumentius. the king who took you in has died and set you free. you could sail home. the queen asks you to stay and help until her son is grown. what do you do?
o: go home. you've been away long enough.
stay and help run the kingdom.
games.why: the brothers stayed. Frumentius used the time to help Christian merchants gather and pray, and only left when the prince came of age.

practice: Of the things you heard today, Abba Salama, the tabot on the altar, the ark the tradition speaks of, choose the one that stays with you, and turn it over gently.
Then let your mind go to the people who carry it every day as their own, in Ethiopia and wherever Ethiopians live now. If you pray, pray for them; if not, just hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Frumentius. The boy who survived a massacre in Ethiopia, served a king, stayed to help a queen, and came back as a bishop. Abba Salama.

orig.note: Ge'ez: tabot, the consecrated tablet on the altar of an Ethiopian Orthodox church.

carryVoice: Your line: the church of the ark. Abba Salama, father of peace, remembered as their own. See you tomorrow.
